title: If not true, don't
hook: if it isn't right, don't do it; if it isn't true, don't say it (Meditations 12.17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: fate, providence, or chaos, and Marcus refusing to bet his calm on which one runs the world. Your line was keep my mind. Which uncertainty did you steady yourself in? Day six hundred thirty-two.

"Love the haircut." "Running five minutes late," sent from the couch. "No, it's fine, really." Most of the small untruths in a day are soft, quick, and meant to keep things moving. Nobody keeps count. Marcus Aurelius, in the last book of his notebook, writes himself a rule so short it fits on a sticky note, and it doesn't leave much room for any of them. Two halves, one about your hands and one about your mouth. Today: two gates.
screen: `LOVE THE HAIRCUT.` → `RUNNING FIVE MINUTES LATE.` → `A RULE FOR HANDS AND MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: "If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it." First, notice the shape. It's not a lecture on honesty. It's a filter with two gates. Before an act, one question: is it right? Before a word, one question: is it true? If the answer is no, you don't need a long debate. You just don't. Second, the Greek. The word for true is alēthes, from the family of alētheia, truth. Truth runs all through the notebook. Back in book three Marcus put it among his four great goods, and in book nine he calls the deliberate lie a kind of impiety, a wrong against nature itself, which he says is also rightly called truth. A lie, even a small one, is a mind saying something it knows isn't so. Third, what the rule doesn't say. It doesn't say: say every true thing. Marcus elsewhere tells himself to be kind, to correct people gently, to keep quiet when quiet is better. The rule is about what never leaves your mouth, not about blurting everything that's in your head. Between the untrue word and the cruel true word, there's a third door: silence, or a smaller true thing. "I'm not sure about the haircut, but you look happy" is true. So is "I'm still on the couch, leaving now." Fourth, why it's at the end. To many readers, book twelve reads like a man packing for a trip. He keeps what's light and what matters. A two-gate rule for every day is the kind of thing you pack.
screen: `TWO GATES: IS IT RIGHT? IS IT TRUE?` · `ALĒTHES: THE GREEK WORD FOR TRUE.` · `NOT EVERY TRUE THING NEEDS SAYING.` · `A RULE LIGHT ENOUGH TO PACK.` · then, large: `IF NOT TRUE, DON'T.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow down. Think back over yesterday. Find one small untrue thing you said: a polite fib, a softened excuse, an "I'm fine." Don't scold yourself. Just look at it. Now picture the same moment again, and find the smaller true thing you could have said instead, or the silence that would have done. Hold that true sentence in mind. Today, when an easy untrue word comes up, you can let it pass without saying it. The bell holds the time.
Two gates. Marcus's rule has one for acts, is it right, and one for words, is it true; if not, don't. Today's word.
Your line: a smaller true thing. Today, catch one easy fib before it leaves your mouth, and swap in your line, or say nothing. Day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often treat 12.17 as a daily check, pausing before an act or a word to ask whether it is right and whether it is true.

original.note: Greek: true. The word Marcus uses in 12.17: if it is not true, do not say it.

trapdoor: what you thought: be honest, a nice slogan.
what it means: a two-gate filter, one for acts and one for words, short enough to use in the moment.
what a scholar hears: the Greek is two tiny clauses, εἰ μὴ καθήκει and εἰ μὴ ἀληθές; and in 9.1 Marcus calls the deliberate lie an impiety, because universal nature is also named truth.

sources.quoted: If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.

notes: Confirm Long 1862's exact wording and punctuation of 12.17 (colon between the halves).
Confirm the Greek of 12.17 uses ἀληθές (εἰ μὴ ἀληθές ἐστι, μὴ εἴπῃς).
Kindness and gentle correction: Meditations 11.18 (the list of reminders on dealing with others). Paraphrased.
The hook's 'sticky note' and haircut examples are illustrative, not from Marcus.

9.1 paraphrased (Long: he who lies is guilty of impiety to the same divinity; this universal nature is named truth, and is the prime cause of all things that are true). Confirm. Confirm the Greek of 12.17's first clause (εἰ μὴ καθήκει, μὴ πράξῃς).
